s: Hector killed Protesilaus after Protesilaus had killed many of the barbarians.

l: death of Protesilaus, The Library, ES 28 | ᾿Αναχθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Τενέδου 1 προσέπλεον
s: The death of Protesilaus occurred after he was the first Greek to land and had killed many barbarians. Laodamia continued to love him, and Hermes later brought him up from Hades before he was returned there.

l: Laodamia, The Library, ES 28 | ᾿Αναχθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Τενέδου 1 προσέπλεον
s: Laodamia loved Protesilaus after his death and made an image resembling him. When Hermes brought Protesilaus up from Hades, she rejoiced on seeing him, but after he was taken back to Hades she stabbed herself to death.

l: Cycnus, The Library, ES 28 | ᾿Αναχθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Τενέδου 1 προσέπλεον
s: Cycnus was killed by Achilles, who threw a stone at his head. After Cycnus died, the barbarians fled into Troy.

l: killing of Cycnus, The Library, ES 28 | ᾿Αναχθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Τενέδου 1 προσέπλεον
s: The killing of Cycnus was carried out by Achilles with a stone thrown at Cycnus's head. It caused the barbarians to flee into Troy.

l: siege of Troy, The Library, ES 28 | ᾿Αναχθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Τενέδου 1 προσέπλεον
s: The siege of Troy began after the Greeks drove the Trojans into the city. The Greeks shut the Trojans inside, drew up their ships, and besieged them.

l: Troilus, The Library, ES 28 | ᾿Αναχθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Τενέδου 1 προσέπλεον
s: Achilles waylaid Troilus in the sanctuary of Thymbraean Apollo and killed him.

l: The Library, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: The unit concerns Achilles’ campaigns around Troy, the arrival of Trojan allies after nine years, and the major battles of the Trojan War. Alexander fights Menelaus but is rescued by Aphrodite, while Diomedes wounds Aphrodite and Ajax fights Hector. The Trojans drive the Greeks behind their wall and set fire to the ships, prompting Achilles to send Patroclus, whose death leads Achilles to return to battle. Achilles kills Hector, and Priam later ransoms Hector’s body and buries it.

l: Achilles, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Achilles captures Lycaon, ravages the country around Troy, seizes many cities, and fights against the Trojans for years. He initially refuses to fight because he is angry over Briseis, but sends Patroclus to battle when the ships are burning. After Patroclus is killed, Achilles receives armor from Hephaestus, returns to battle, kills many Trojans including Asteropaeus and Hector, and drags Hector’s body to the ships.

l: Troy, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Troy is defended by allies who arrive after nine years. Its forces drive the Greeks behind their wall, breach the wall, and set fire to the ships.

l: Trojan allies, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Trojan allies arrive from surrounding cities after nine years. They include forces led by Aeneas, Acamas, Theanus, Pyraechmes, Pylaemenes, Pandarus, Adrastus, Amphius, Asius, Hippothous, Chromius, Ennomus, Odius, Epistrophus, Phorcys, Ascanius, Mesthles, Antiphus, Nastes, Amphimachus, Sarpedon, and Glaucus.

l: Sarpedon, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Sarpedon, son of Zeus, fights among the Trojan allies. Patroclus kills him.

l: Glaucus, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Glaucus, son of Hippolochus, comes as an ally of the Trojans. When he encounters Diomedes, Diomedes recalls the friendship between their fathers and exchanges arms with him.

l: Alexander, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Alexander fights Menelaus in single combat. When he is being defeated, Aphrodite carries him away.

l: Menelaus, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Menelaus fights Alexander in single combat. Pandarus wounds him with an arrow, breaking the oaths.

l: Aphrodite, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Aphrodite rescues Alexander when he is losing his single combat with Menelaus. Later, while helping Aeneas, she is wounded by Diomedes.

l: Diomedes, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Diomedes wounds Aphrodite while she is helping Aeneas. He recognizes the friendship between his father and Glaucus and exchanges arms with Glaucus. He later joins Ulysses as a spy and kills Dolon and Rhesus.

l: Hector, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Hector challenges the bravest warrior to single combat, and Ajax is chosen to fight him. He later breaches the Greek wall, sets fire to the ships, kills Patroclus after Patroclus has been wounded by Euphorbus, and is eventually killed by Achilles.

l: Ajax, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Ajax is chosen by lot to fight Hector in single combat, and the heralds separate them when night falls. He later helps defend the Greek ships and, after a fierce battle, rescues Patroclus’ body.

l: Greeks, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: The Greeks build a wall and ditch by the ships. They are driven behind the wall by the Trojans, send an embassy to Achilles, and later send Ulysses and Diomedes as spies. Their forces suffer heavy losses and the ships are set on fire before Achilles returns to battle.

l: Trojans, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: The Trojans gain confidence when Achilles refuses to fight and come out from the city. They drive the Greeks to their wall, breach it, and burn the ships, but later flee when Patroclus appears wearing Achilles’ armor and are pursued by Achilles.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Ulysses goes with Phoenix and Ajax as an embassy to Achilles, asking him to fight and promising Briseis and other gifts. He later joins Diomedes as a spy, and together they kill Dolon and Rhesus and take the horses.

l: Patroclus, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Patroclus is sent by Achilles to defend the burning ships, wearing Achilles’ armor and driving his horses. The Trojans flee from him, but after he kills Sarpedon and many others, he is wounded by Euphorbus and killed by Hector. Achilles later holds funeral games for him.

l: Briseis, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: Briseis is the reason Achilles refuses to fight. The Greeks promise to return her to Achilles, and Achilles later recovers her after laying aside his anger.

l: Trojan War, The Library, Λυκάονα λαμβάνει. παραλαβὼν δὲ ᾿Αχιλλεύς
s: During the Trojan War, Achilles campaigns against cities around Troy, while Trojan allies arrive after nine years. The fighting includes the single combat between Alexander and Menelaus, the battles involving Diomedes, Ajax, Hector, Patroclus, and Achilles, and the burning of the Greek ships. The unit ends with Priam ransoming Hector’s body from Achilles and burying it.

s: Penthesilia, daughter of Otrere and Ares, accidentally killed Hippolyte, was purified by Priam, and later killed many in battle before Achilles killed her; Achilles then killed Thersites after falling in love with her after death. Achilles was buried with Patroclus in the White Isle, and games were held in his honour. Ajax and Odysseus then competed for Achilles’ arms; Odysseus won, Ajax went mad, slaughtered cattle and their herdsmen, and killed himself.

l: Penthesilia, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Penthesilia, daughter of Otrere and Ares, accidentally killed Hippolyte and was purified by Priam. In battle she killed many, including Machaon, and was later killed by Achilles; after her death Achilles fell in love with her and killed Thersites for mocking him.

l: Hippolyte, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Hippolyte was the mother of Hippolytus and was also called Glauce and Melanippe. During Phaedra’s wedding she appeared armed with Amazons and threatened to kill Theseus’s guests; in the ensuing battle she died, either accidentally at the hands of Penthesilia, by Theseus, or after Theseus’s men trapped and killed her.

l: Achilles, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Achilles killed Penthesilia and later killed Memnon. He was shot in the ankle by Alexander and Apollo at the Scaean gate, was buried with Patroclus in the White Isle, and was said to consort with Medea in the Isles of the Blest after death.

l: Amazons, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: The Amazons accompanied Hippolyte when she appeared armed at Phaedra’s wedding and threatened Theseus’s guests. A battle followed, and Hippolyte died.

l: Memnon, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Memnon, son of Tithonus and the Dawn, came to Troy with a great force of Ethiopians. He killed many Achaeans, including Antilochus, and was then killed by Achilles.

l: Ajax, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Ajax carried Achilles’ body through the enemy while Odysseus fought those attacking him. He competed with Odysseus for Achilles’ arms, lost the contest, became mad, slaughtered cattle and their herdsmen while mistaking them for Achaeans, and later killed himself.

l: Ulysses, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Odysseus fought the enemy while Ajax carried Achilles’ body through them. He competed with Ajax for Achilles’ arms and was chosen as the winner.

l: Greeks, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: The Achaeans fought at Troy and suffered deaths at the hands of Memnon. Ajax, while mad, mistook cattle and their herdsmen for Achaeans and slaughtered them.

l: Trojans, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: The Trojans were pursued by Achilles after Memnon’s death. They, or according to some accounts the allies, judged the contest between Ajax and Odysseus and preferred Odysseus.

l: Troy, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Troy was the place to which Memnon came with the Ethiopians against the Greeks. It was also the setting for the battles involving Memnon, Achilles, Ajax, and the other forces.

l: White Isle, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: The White Isle was the place where Achilles was buried with Patroclus, with their bones mixed together.

l: battle involving Penthesilia, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: After Priam purified Penthesilia, a battle took place in which she killed many people, including Machaon, before Achilles killed her.

l: death of Penthesilia, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Penthesilia was killed by Achilles after she had killed many in battle. Achilles fell in love with her after her death and killed Thersites for jeering at him.

l: arrival of Memnon at Troy, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Memnon arrived at Troy with a great force of Ethiopians to fight against the Greeks. He killed many Greeks, including Antilochus, before Achilles killed him.

l: death of Achilles, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Achilles was shot in the ankle by Alexander and Apollo at the Scaean gate. He was buried with Patroclus in the White Isle, and games were held in his honour.

l: contest for Achilles' arms, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Achilles’ arms were offered as a prize to the bravest, and Ajax and Odysseus competed for them. The Trojans, or according to some the allies, judged the contest and awarded victory to Odysseus.

l: Achilles' arms, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: Achilles’ arms were set up as a prize for the bravest after his death. They were awarded to Odysseus rather than Ajax.

l: suicide of Ajax, The Library, V. | "Ore Πενθεσίλεια, ᾿Οτρηρῆς καὶ ἔΑρεος,
s: After losing the contest for Achilles’ arms, Ajax became disturbed with grief and planned a nighttime attack on the army. Athena drove him mad, and after he recovered his senses from slaughtering cattle and their herdsmen, he killed himself.

l: Trojan War, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: The Trojan War had lasted ten years, and the Greeks were becoming despondent.

l: Greeks, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: The Greeks learned from Calchas and Helenus what was required to take Troy. They obtained the bones of Pelops, brought Neoptolemus from Scyros, and stole the Palladium.

l: Trojans, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: The Trojans were opposed by Neoptolemus, who killed many of them. They were also defended by Eurypylus and guarded the Palladium in their city.

l: Calchas, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Calchas prophesied that Troy could not be taken unless the Greeks had the bow and arrows of Hercules fighting on their side. He also said that Helenus knew the oracles protecting the city.

l: Troy, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Troy could not be taken while the Palladium remained inside it. Its capture also required the bones of Pelops and the aid of Neoptolemus.

l: Ilium, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Helenus revealed how Ilium could be taken: the bones of Pelops had to be brought to the Greeks, Neoptolemus had to fight for them, and the Palladium had to be stolen.

l: bow and arrows of Hercules, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Calchas said that the Greeks could not take Troy unless they had the bow and arrows of Hercules fighting on their side.

l: Ulysses, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Odysseus went with Diomedes to Lemnos and by craft obtained the bow and arrows of Hercules from Philoctetes, persuading him to sail to Troy. He later captured Helenus and, with Diomedes, entered the Trojan city by night and stole the Palladium with Helen's help.

l: Diomedes, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Diomedes accompanied Odysseus to Lemnos and later joined him in entering the Trojan city and carrying the Palladium to the ships.

l: Lemnos, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Odysseus and Diomedes went to Lemnos to obtain the bow and arrows of Hercules from Philoctetes.

l: Philoctetes, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Philoctetes was persuaded by Odysseus to sail from Lemnos to Troy after Odysseus had obtained his bow and arrows by craft. He was healed by Podalirius and then killed Alexander.

l: Alexander, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Alexander was shot and killed by the healed Philoctetes.

l: Helenus, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: After Deiphobus was preferred over him in marriage to Helen, Helenus left Troy and stayed on Ida. Odysseus captured him and brought him to the Greek camp, where he was forced to reveal how Ilium could be taken.

l: Deiphobus, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Deiphobus quarrelled with Helenus over marriage to Helen and was preferred over him.

l: Helen, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Helen recognized Odysseus when he entered the Trojan city in disguise and helped him steal the Palladium.

l: oracles protecting Troy, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Helenus was said to know the oracles that protected Troy. Under compulsion, he revealed the conditions for taking Ilium.

l: Pelops, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: The Greeks were told that the bones of Pelops had to be brought to them before Ilium could be taken.

l: bones of Pelops, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: The Greeks caused the bones of Pelops to be brought to them as one of the conditions for taking Ilium.

l: Neoptolemus, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Neoptolemus was required to fight for the Greeks. Odysseus and Phoenix persuaded Lycomedes at Scyros to let him go, and Neoptolemus later killed many Trojans and Eurypylus.

l: Palladium, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Helenus said that the Palladium, which had fallen from heaven, had to be stolen because Troy could not be taken while it remained inside the city. Odysseus and Diomedes stole it from the Trojan city and carried it to the ships.

l: Scyros, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Odysseus and Phoenix went to Scyros and persuaded Lycomedes to let Neoptolemus go to the Greek camp.

l: Eurypylus, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Eurypylus, son of Telephus, arrived to aid the Trojans with a large force of Mysians. After performing great deeds, he was killed by Neoptolemus.

l: Trojan city, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Odysseus entered the Trojan city at night in disguise as a beggar. With Helen's help, he stole the Palladium and, after killing many guards, carried it to the ships with Diomedes.

l: Greek expedition to Lemnos, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Odysseus and Diomedes undertook the expedition to Lemnos to obtain the bow and arrows of Hercules from Philoctetes.

l: healing of Philoctetes, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Philoctetes was healed by Podalirius after arriving at Troy.

l: death of Alexander, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Alexander died after Philoctetes shot him with the bow and arrows of Hercules.

l: capture of Helenus, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Odysseus waylaid and captured Helenus and brought him to the Greek camp. Helenus was then forced to reveal how Ilium could be taken.

l: theft of the Palladium, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Odysseus and Diomedes entered the Trojan city at night, stole the Palladium with Helen's help, killed many of its guards, and carried it to the ships.

l: death of Eurypylus, The Library, E 8 |’ ‘Hoy δὲ ὄντος τοῦ πολέμου δεκαετοῦς ἀθυμοῦσι
s: Eurypylus was killed by Neoptolemus after arriving with a large Mysian force to aid the Trojans.

Cassandra and Laocoon warn that armed men are inside, but the Trojans disregard them after serpents sent by Apollo devour Laocoon’s sons. That night the Greeks emerge, open the gates, and admit their returning forces, who sack and burn Troy.

l: Wooden Horse, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Epeus constructs the Wooden Horse with a hollow interior and openings in its sides. Greek warriors enter it, and the Trojans drag it into Troy and place it beside Priam’s palace as a supposed sacred offering.

l: Ulysses, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Ulysses persuades fifty of the best Greek warriors, or three thousand according to the author of the Little Iliad, to enter the Wooden Horse and is appointed their leader. He holds Anticlus’s mouth shut when Anticlus is about to answer Helen’s call, then emerges from the horse with the other Greeks and helps open the gates of Troy.

l: Greeks, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: The Greeks hide their best warriors in the Wooden Horse, burn their tents, and sail to Tenedos. They return by night, enter Troy through the opened gates, kill the sleeping Trojans, burn the city, and divide the spoils.

l: Tenedos, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: The Greeks sail to Tenedos and lie offshore after leaving Sinon behind. They later sail back from Tenedos to Troy after Sinon gives the agreed signal.

l: Trojans, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: The Trojans see the Greek camp deserted and believe that the Greeks have fled. They bring the Wooden Horse into Troy, disregard warnings that it contains armed men, and feast before the Greeks emerge and attack them during the night.

l: Sinon, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Sinon remains behind after the Greeks sail away and is meant to light a beacon as their signal. When the Greeks approach from Tenedos, he lights the beacon from the tomb of Achilles.

l: Cassandra, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Cassandra says that an armed force is inside the Wooden Horse, but the Trojans do not follow her warning. Later, Ajax the Locrian finds her clinging to the image of Athena and uses violence against her.

l: Laocoon, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Laocoon, described as a seer, also warns that the Wooden Horse contains an armed force. Apollo sends two serpents from nearby islands, and they devour Laocoon’s sons.

l: Troy, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Troy is entered by the Greeks after they emerge from the Wooden Horse and open the gates. The Greeks kill the inhabitants, burn the city, and carry away its spoils.

l: Priam, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Priam takes refuge at the altar of Zeus of the Courtyard. Neoptolemus kills him there during the Greek attack.

l: Menelaus, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Menelaus and Ulysses recognize Glaucus, son of Antenor, and rescue him when he flees to his house. Menelaus kills Deiphobus and leads Helen to the ships.

l: Aeneas, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Aeneas carries his father Anchises away from Troy as he flees. The Greeks let him escape because of his piety.

l: Helen, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: Helen walks around the Wooden Horse and calls the Greek leaders by imitating the voices of their wives. Menelaus later kills Deiphobus and takes Helen to the ships.

l: Sack of Ilium, The Library, But afterwards he invented the construction of
s: The fall of Troy begins when the Greeks use the Wooden Horse to enter the city and open its gates to their returning forces. The Greeks then kill the sleeping Trojans, burn Troy, divide the spoils, kill Priam, and carry away captives including Helen.

l: The Library, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Ajax the Locrian violated Cassandra while she clung to Athena’s wooden image, which thereafter was said to look upward in horror. The Trojans were slain, Troy was burned, its spoil was divided, and Astyanax was thrown from the battlements while Polyxena was sacrificed on Achilles’ grave. Agamemnon received Cassandra, Neoptolemus received Andromache, and Ulysses received Hecuba, although another account gives Hecuba to Helenus and says she became a bitch. Laodice was swallowed by a chasm in the earth before everyone.

l: Ajax son of Oileus, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Ajax the Locrian violated Cassandra while she clung to the wooden image of Athena.

l: Cassandra, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Cassandra was violated by Ajax the Locrian while clinging to Athena’s wooden image. Agamemnon later received her as a special award.

l: Trojans, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: The Trojans were slain after the capture of Troy.

l: Troy, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Troy was set on fire after the Trojans were slain, and its spoil was divided among the Greeks.

l: Astyanax, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Astyanax was thrown from the battlements after the capture of Troy. The text’s notes report differing traditions about whether Ulysses or Neoptolemus killed him.

l: Polyxena, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Polyxena was slaughtered on the grave of Achilles.

l: Achilles, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Achilles’ grave was the place where Polyxena was sacrificed. The notes report traditions in which Achilles’ ghost demanded or otherwise prompted the sacrifice.

l: Agamemnon, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Agamemnon received Cassandra as a special award after the sack of Troy.

l: Neoptolemus, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Neoptolemus received Andromache as a special award. Some traditions in the notes say that he threw Astyanax from the battlements or slew Polyxena on Achilles’ grave.

l: Ulysses, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Ulysses received Hecuba as a special award. The notes also report traditions in which he killed or threw Astyanax from a tower.

l: Andromache, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Andromache was awarded to Neoptolemus after the sack of Troy.

l: Hecuba, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Hecuba was awarded to Ulysses, although some said Helenus received her and took her to the Chersonese. There she was said to become a bitch, which Helenus buried at the place called the Bitch’s Tomb.

l: Helenus, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Some accounts say that Helenus received Hecuba, crossed with her to the Chersonese, and buried her after she became a bitch.

l: Greeks, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: The Greeks divided the spoil of Troy among themselves and sacrificed to all the gods. According to some accounts, they later decreed Astyanax’s death in a formal assembly.

l: Sack of Ilium, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: During and after the sack of Troy, its inhabitants were slain, the city was burned, its spoil was divided, Astyanax was killed, and Polyxena was sacrificed.

l: sacrifice of Polyxena, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: The sacrifice of Polyxena took place on the grave of Achilles. The notes give traditions in which Achilles’ ghost demanded the sacrifice and in which Neoptolemus performed it.

l: death of Astyanax, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Astyanax’s death is described as a fall from the battlements. The notes preserve differing accounts naming Ulysses or Neoptolemus as the agent and differing accounts about whether the killing occurred during the sack or afterward by decree.

l: Achilles’ grave, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Achilles’ grave was the site of Polyxena’s slaughter.

l: Hecuba’s transformation, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Hecuba’s transformation into a bitch is reported as an alternative tradition. In that account, Helenus took her to the Chersonese, where she was buried at the Bitch’s Tomb.

l: Apollodorus, The Library, EPITOME, v. 22-23
s: Apollodorus’s account records the sack of Troy, the killing of Astyanax, the sacrifice of Polyxena, and the distribution of the captive women among the Greek leaders. The notes compare his account with several other traditions.

l: The Library, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: After Troy was laid waste, Calchas said that Athena was angry because of Ajax's impiety, but Ajax fled to an altar and was spared. Agamemnon and Menelaus quarrelled about whether to sail or remain and sacrifice to Athena; Menelaus later reached Egypt after a storm, while Diomedes and Nestor had a prosperous voyage. Calchas travelled with Amphilochus, Leonteus, Podalirius, and Polypoetes to Colophon, where Mopsus surpassed him in divination, and Calchas died and was buried at Notium. Athena sent a storm against the Greeks, Ajax perished after Poseidon split the rock where he had survived, and Nauplius used beacon fires to lure Greek ships onto the Capherian rocks after arranging punishments for those connected with Palamedes's death.

l: Troy, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Troy was laid waste before the Greeks were about to sail away.

l: Ajax, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Because of Ajax's impiety, Calchas said that Athena was angry with the Greeks. Ajax fled to an altar and was spared; later Athena struck his ship with a thunderbolt, he survived on a rock, but Poseidon split the rock with his trident and Ajax fell into the sea and died. Thetis buried his washed-up body at Myconos.

l: Athena, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Calchas said that Athena was angry with the Greeks because of Ajax's impiety. She later sent a storm against the Greeks at the request of Athena herself to Zeus, struck Ajax's ship with a thunderbolt, and caused many ships to founder.

l: Calchas, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Calchas detained the Greeks after Troy was laid waste, saying that Athena was angry because of Ajax's impiety. He travelled to Colophon, where he competed with Mopsus in divination; after Mopsus correctly answered riddles about a fig tree and a pregnant sow, Calchas died and was buried at Notium.

l: Agamemnon, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Agamemnon quarrelled with Menelaus and ordered that they remain and sacrifice to Athena. He later sacrificed and sailed, stopping at Tenedos. He had been an accomplice of Ulysses in the killing of Palamedes, and the Greeks favoured him when Nauplius sought satisfaction.

l: Menelaus, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Menelaus advised sailing away rather than remaining to sacrifice to Athena. He sailed with Diomedes and Nestor, but a storm overtook him; after losing the rest of his ships, he reached Egypt with five ships.

l: Diomedes, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Diomedes sailed with Nestor and Menelaus. He and Nestor had a prosperous voyage, unlike Menelaus.

l: Nestor, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Nestor sailed with Diomedes and Menelaus. He and Diomedes had a prosperous voyage.

l: Mopsus, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Mopsus, the son of Apollo and Manto, received Calchas and his companions at Colophon and disputed with Calchas about divination. He correctly said that a wild fig tree bore ten thousand figs, a bushel, and one extra, and that a pregnant sow carried nine male piglets to be born the next day at the sixth hour.

l: storm against the Greeks, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: The storm against the Greeks was sent by Zeus at Athena's request. It struck the Greeks near Tenos, causing many ships to founder and separating Menelaus from the others.

l: Greek ships, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Many Greek ships foundered in the storm near Tenos. Menelaus lost the rest of his ships before reaching Egypt with five ships, and other Greek ships were later lured toward the Capherian rocks by a beacon fire and wrecked.

l: Nauplius, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Nauplius was the son of Clymene and the father of Palamedes. After Palamedes was killed, Nauplius unsuccessfully demanded satisfaction from the Greeks, arranged for Greek wives to be unfaithful, and later lit a beacon fire on Mount Caphareus to lure returning Greeks to destruction.

l: Caphereus, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Nauplius lit a beacon fire on Mount Caphareus, which was also called Xylophagus, to deceive returning Greek ships into approaching the shore as though it were a harbour.

l: shipwreck of the Greeks at Caphereus, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Greek ships that approached the beacon fire, believing it indicated a harbour, were wrecked at the Capherian rocks, and many men died.

l: Palamedes, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Palamedes, the son of Nauplius and Clymene, was stoned to death through the machinations of Ulysses, with Agamemnon as his accomplice. His death prompted Nauplius to seek satisfaction from the Greeks and to take revenge.

l: Ulysses, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Ulysses was involved with Agamemnon in the killing of Palamedes. Nauplius later retaliated after the Greeks refused to provide satisfaction for Palamedes's death.

l: Greeks, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: The Greeks quarrelled over whether to sail or remain and sacrifice to Athena, then departed in different groups. Athena sent a storm against them, many of their ships were lost, and returning Greeks were later deceived by Nauplius's beacon fire and wrecked.

l: beacon fire, The Library, ἔμελλον ἀποπλεῖν πορθήσαντες Τροίαν, ὑ ὑπὸ Κάλ-
s: Nauplius lit a beacon fire on Mount Caphareus to make the returning Greeks believe that a harbour was nearby. The Greeks approached it and were wrecked on the Capherian rocks.

l: The Library, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Neoptolemus remained in Tenedos for two days on the advice of Thetis, then traveled by land to Molossia with Helenus. After Phoenix died on the way, Neoptolemus buried him, defeated the Molossians, became their king, and fathered Molossus with Andromache. Helenus founded a city in Molossia and married Deidamia, while Neoptolemus later took Hermione from Orestes and was killed at Delphi. Another account says that Neoptolemus was killed by Machaereus after attacking Apollo’s sanctuary.

l: Neoptolemus, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Neoptolemus stayed in Tenedos for two days on Thetis’s advice, then traveled by land to Molossia with Helenus. He buried Phoenix, defeated the Molossians, became king, and fathered Molossus with Andromache. After Peleus was expelled and died, Neoptolemus succeeded to his father’s kingdom; he later took Hermione from Orestes and was killed at Delphi.

l: Thetis, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Thetis advised Neoptolemus to remain in Tenedos for two days before traveling to Molossia.

l: Helenus, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Helenus traveled with Neoptolemus to Molossia and later founded and inhabited a city there. Neoptolemus gave him Deidamia as his wife.

l: Molossians, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: The Molossians were defeated by Neoptolemus in battle, after which he became their king.

l: Molossia, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Molossia was the country to which Neoptolemus traveled by land with Helenus. Helenus founded a city there, and Neoptolemus ruled the Molossians there as king.

l: Andromache, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Andromache bore Molossus to Neoptolemus.

l: Peleus, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Peleus was expelled from Phthia by the sons of Acastus and died. After his death, Neoptolemus succeeded to his father’s kingdom.

l: Orestes, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Orestes went mad, and Neoptolemus took his wife Hermione, who had previously been betrothed to Neoptolemus in Troy. Orestes is said to have killed Neoptolemus at Delphi.

l: Hermione, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Hermione was Orestes’s wife and had previously been betrothed to Neoptolemus in Troy. When Orestes went mad, Neoptolemus took her.

l: Delphi, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Neoptolemus was killed at Delphi. In another account, he went to Delphi to demand satisfaction from Apollo for his father’s death, plundered the votive offerings, and burned the temple.

l: Apollo, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: According to one account, Neoptolemus went to Apollo at Delphi to demand satisfaction for his father’s death, then plundered the votive offerings and burned the temple.

l: Machaereus, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Machaereus, a Phocian, is said to have killed Neoptolemus after Neoptolemus plundered Apollo’s votive offerings and burned the temple at Delphi.

l: Peleus’s exile, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Peleus was expelled from Phthia by the sons of Acastus and subsequently died. Neoptolemus then succeeded to his father’s kingdom.

l: Neoptolemus’s journey to Molossia, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: After remaining in Tenedos for two days on Thetis’s advice, Neoptolemus traveled by land to Molossia with Helenus. Phoenix died along the way, and Neoptolemus buried him.

l: Neoptolemus’s conquest of Molossia, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Neoptolemus defeated the Molossians in battle and became their king.

l: marriage of Neoptolemus and Hermione, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Neoptolemus took Hermione, who had previously been betrothed to him in Troy, from Orestes when Orestes went mad.

l: Neoptolemus’s death at Delphi, The Library, 12 Νεοπτόλεμος δὲ μείνας ἐν Τενέδῳ δύο ἡμέρας
s: Neoptolemus was killed at Delphi, according to the main account, by Orestes. Another account says that Machaereus killed him after he demanded satisfaction from Apollo, plundered the votive offerings, and burned the temple.

l: The Library, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: After the Trojan War, the Greeks were scattered to Libya, Italy, Sicily, Iberian islands, the Sangarius River, Cyprus, and other places. Antiphus son of Thessalus settled among the Pelasgians and named the country Thessaly, while Philoctetes settled in Crimissa in Italy and Demophon eventually settled in Cyprus after the death of Phyllis. Podalirius settled in the Carian Chersonese, and Amphilochus son of Alcmaeon and Mopsus killed each other in a contest for kingship. After a plague struck Locris, the Locrians sent two maidens to serve Athena at Ilium for a thousand years.

l: ancient Greeks, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: After their wanderings and shipwrecks, the Greeks settled in Libya, Italy, Sicily, the islands near Iberia, along the Sangarius River, Cyprus, Crete, and other places. Some Greeks who lost their ships after the Trojan War settled in Italy with the daughters of Laomedon.

l: Italy, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Italy received several Greek refugees, including Philoctetes, who settled at Crimissa, and Greeks whose ships were burned by the daughters of Laomedon. The river Navaethus was in Italy.

l: Cyprus, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Agapenor, Phidippus with the Coans, and Demophon with his followers settled in Cyprus. Demophon went there after leaving Phyllis, and his followers settled there after his death.

l: Antiphus son of Thessalus, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Antiphus went to the Pelasgians, took possession of their country, and called it Thessaly.

l: Thessaly, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Thessaly was the name Antiphus son of Thessalus gave to the country he took possession of among the Pelasgians.

l: Philoctetes, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Philoctetes was driven to Italy among the Campanians, fought the Lucanians near Croton and Thurium, and settled at Crimissa. He founded a sanctuary of Apollo Alaios and dedicated his bow there.

l: Demophon, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Demophon arrived with a few ships among the Thracian Bisaltians and married Phyllis, receiving the kingdom as her dowry. He left for his homeland after promising to return, went to Cyprus, and died after opening the casket of Mother Rhea, falling on his sword when his horse stumbled.

l: Phyllis, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Phyllis, daughter of the king of the Bisaltians, fell in love with Demophon and married him. After he failed to return within the appointed time, she cursed him and killed herself.

l: casket of Mother Rhea, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Phyllis gave Demophon the casket of Mother Rhea and told him not to open it until he had abandoned hope of returning to her. When Demophon opened it, he was seized by fear and died while riding.

l: Podalirius, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Podalirius consulted the oracle at Delphi about where to settle. He settled in the Carian Chersonese at a place surrounded by mountains, where he would suffer no harm even if the encompassing heaven fell.

l: Amphilochus, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Amphilochus son of Alcmaeon was, according to some, driven by a storm to Mopsus. The two fought a single combat for the kingdom and killed each other.

l: Mopsus, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Mopsus received Amphilochus son of Alcmaeon after the latter was driven to him by a storm. According to one account, Mopsus and Amphilochus killed each other while fighting for the kingdom.

l: Troy, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Troy was the destination of the two Locrian maidens sent to propitiate Athena. The maidens were pursued by the inhabitants of Troy and took refuge in the sanctuary.

l: Locrians, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: The Locrians returned to their country with difficulty and, after a plague struck Locris, received an oracle directing them to propitiate Athena at Ilium. They sent two maidens as suppliants for a thousand years.

l: Locris, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Locris was afflicted by a plague three years after the Locrians regained their country. The Locrians then sent maidens to Troy in accordance with an oracle.

l: plague in Locris, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: The plague occurred in Locris three years after the Locrians returned there. It led the Locrians to seek an oracle and send two maidens to Athena at Ilium.

l: Athena, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: Athena at Ilium was to be propitiated by the Locrians after the plague in Locris. Two maidens were sent as suppliants to her for a thousand years.

l: Athena’s sanctuary, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: The two Locrian maidens took refuge in the sanctuary after being pursued by the inhabitants of Troy. They did not approach Athena, but swept and sprinkled the sanctuary, remained inside it, wore single garments, and had cropped hair.

l: Locrian maidens sent to Troy, The Library, ΕἸ [Ὅτι πλανηθέντες “Ελληνες ἄλλοι ἀλλαχοῦ
s: The first two maidens were Periboea and Cleopatra, chosen by lot and sent to Troy as suppliants for a thousand years. After the first maidens died, others were sent; later, infants with nurses were sent, and the practice ended after a thousand years following the Phocian War.

l: The Library, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: Agamemnon returns to Mycenae with Cassandra but is murdered by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra, who then rule Mycenae. Electra saves Orestes and sends him to Strophius, and Orestes later kills his mother and Aegisthus after receiving divine permission to avenge his father. Orestes is pursued by the Furies, acquitted at the Areopagus, and sent to the Taurians to bring back their wooden image; he escapes with his sister, who serves as priestess there. Menelaus wanders for eight years before returning to Mycenae and then recovers his kingdom at Sparta with Helen.

l: Agamemnon, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: Agamemnon returns to Mycenae with Cassandra. Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra murder him with a sleeveless, neckless shirt, and Cassandra is killed as well.

l: Aegisthus, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: Aegisthus participates with Clytaemnestra in the murder of Agamemnon and Cassandra. He then reigns over Mycenae until Orestes kills him.

l: Clytaemnestra, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: Clytaemnestra gives Agamemnon a shirt without sleeves or a neck, enabling his murder, and participates in killing him and Cassandra. Orestes later kills her.

l: Mycenae, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: Mycenae is where Agamemnon is murdered and where Aegisthus subsequently reigns. Orestes later returns there secretly with Pylades and kills Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra.

l: murder of Agamemnon, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: The murder of Agamemnon is carried out by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra at Mycenae. Orestes later takes vengeance on those responsible.

l: Electra, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: Electra, one of Agamemnon’s daughters, rescues Orestes and entrusts him to Strophius in Phocis. Later, Orestes gives her in marriage to Pylades.

l: Orestes, The Library, ES 23 [᾿Αγαμέμνων δὲ καταντήσας εἰς Μυκήνας μετὰ
s: Orestes is raised by Strophius with Pylades and later asks the god whether he should avenge Agamemnon. With Pylades, he kills Clytaemnestra and Aegisthus, is pursued by the Furies, is acquitted at the Areopagus, and later travels to the Taurians to retrieve their wooden image. He escapes with his sister, marries Hermione or, according to some, Erigone, fathers Tisamenus, and is killed by a snakebite at Oresteum in Arcadia.

l: Poseidon, The Library, VII. ‘O δὲ Ὀδυσσεύς, ὡς μὲν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν,

s: Aeolus is king of Aeolia and, by Zeus's appointment, keeper of the winds. He entertains Odysseus, gives him an ox-hide bag containing the winds, and later drives him from the island when the gods oppose his return.

l: Circe, The Library, VII. ‘O δὲ Ὀδυσσεύς, ὡς μὲν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν,
s: Circe, daughter of Helios and Perse and sister of Aeetes, inhabits the Aeaean isle and knows all enchantments. She transforms Odysseus's companions into animals, restores them after Odysseus resists her magic, and later sends Odysseus on his way.

l: Ilium, The Library, VII. ‘O δὲ Ὀδυσσεύς, ὡς μὲν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν,

s: Polyphemus's cave is near the sea and contains his flocks. Odysseus and twelve companions enter it, become trapped by a huge stone, and escape only after Odysseus blinds Polyphemus.

s: The Aeaean isle is inhabited by Circe. Odysseus reaches it with the one ship that survives the attack of the Laestrygones.

s: Odysseus's companions taste the lotus and must be dragged back to the ships. Some are eaten by Polyphemus, others are swept away when the winds are released, and twenty-two companions who go to Circe are transformed into animals before being restored.

s: Odysseus initially sails with several ships, leaving the others at a neighboring island before approaching the land of the Cyclopes with one ship. The remaining ships are later destroyed by the Laestrygones, leaving only one to reach the Aeaean isle.

s: Circe mixes an enchantment into a drink of cheese, honey, barley meal, and wine. After the companions drink, she touches them with a wand and changes them into wolves, swine, asses, and lions, but later restores them.

s: Ulysses passes the Sirens, Scylla, and Charybdis, reaches Thrinacia, loses his ship after his companions slaughter the Sun’s cattle, and eventually arrives at Ogygia and then among the Phaeacians. With the help of Telemachus, Eumaeus, and Philoetius, Ulysses kills the suitors and returns to Penelope and Laertes. He later follows Tiresias’s directions, propitiates Poseidon among the Thesprotians, and remains there with Callidice before returning to Ithaca.

l: Ulysses, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Ulysses has his companions’ ears stopped with wax and is bound to the mast so that he can hear the Sirens without remaining with them. He passes Scylla and Charybdis, reaches Thrinacia, loses his ship after Zeus strikes it, and drifts to Ogygia. After five years with Calypso, he reaches the Phaeacians, returns to Ithaca in disguise, kills the suitors, and later travels to the Thesprotians according to Tiresias’s directions.

l: Sirens, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: The Sirens are Pisinoe, Aglaope, and Thelxiepia, daughters of Achelous and Melpomene. One plays the lyre, one sings, and one plays the flute; they persuade passing sailors to linger. They have bird forms from the thighs and die after a ship passes them.

l: Circe, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Circe advises Ulysses to stop his companions’ ears with wax and have himself bound to the mast when passing the Sirens. She later advises him to avoid the passage by the Wandering Rocks.

l: Wandering Rocks, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: The Wandering Rocks lie on one side of the route after the Sirens. By Circe’s advice, Ulysses avoids passing between them.

l: Scylla, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Scylla occupies one of two huge cliffs and is described as having a woman’s face and breast, six dog heads, and twelve dog feet. As Ulysses passes, she seizes six of his companions and eats them.

l: Charybdis, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Charybdis occupies the other cliff and draws up and releases the water three times a day. After Ulysses’s ship is destroyed, she swallows the mast, but Ulysses survives by clinging to an overhanging wild fig tree and later recovering the mast.

l: Thrinacia, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Thrinacia is the island of the Sun where cattle graze. Ulysses is detained there by lack of wind, and his companions slaughter some of the cattle for food.

l: Sun, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: The Sun owns the cattle grazing on Thrinacia. After Ulysses’s companions slaughter and eat some of them, the Sun reports the deed to Zeus.

l: Zeus, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Zeus strikes Ulysses’s ship with a thunderbolt after the Sun reports that Ulysses’s companions slaughtered the cattle on Thrinacia.

l: Ogygia, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Ogygia is the island to which Ulysses is carried after escaping Charybdis. Calypso receives him there.

l: Calypso, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Calypso, the daughter of Atlas, receives Ulysses on Ogygia and bears him a son, Latinus. Ulysses remains with her for five years before building a raft and sailing away.

l: Phaeacians, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: The Phaeacians receive Ulysses after Poseidon’s anger breaks apart his raft. Alcinous entertains him, gives him gifts, and sends him with a convoy to his native land.

l: Ithaca, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Ithaca is Ulysses’s native land, where he finds his household wasted and the suitors pursuing Penelope. After killing the suitors, Ulysses later returns there from the land of the Thesprotians and finds that Penelope has borne him a son, Polypoethes.

l: Penelope, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Penelope is pressured to marry because the suitors believe Ulysses is dead. She promises to marry after finishing Laertes’s shroud, later recognizes Ulysses after he kills the suitors, and bears him a son named Polypoethes.

l: Odysseus’s suitors, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: The suitors consume Ulysses’s herds while feasting in his palace and press Penelope to marry. Ulysses, with the help of Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Telemachus, kills them after none can bend the bow of Ulysses.

l: Eumaeus, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Eumaeus receives Ulysses when he arrives disguised as a beggar. Ulysses reveals himself to him, and Eumaeus helps Ulysses, Philoetius, and Telemachus plot against and kill the suitors.

l: Telemachus, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Ulysses reveals himself to Telemachus after arriving in disguise. Telemachus joins Ulysses, Eumaeus, and Philoetius in plotting against the suitors and helps kill them.

l: bow of Ulysses, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Penelope presents the bow of Ulysses to the suitors and declares that she will live with the man who can bend it. None of the suitors can bend it, but Ulysses takes it and uses it to shoot them.

l: Tiresias, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: After the slaughter of the suitors, Ulysses sacrifices to Hades, Persephone, and Tiresias. He then travels to the Thesprotians and offers sacrifice according to Tiresias’s directions in order to propitiate Poseidon.

l: Thesprotians, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: The Thesprotians receive Ulysses after he travels on foot through Epirus. Their queen Callidice asks him to remain and offers him the kingdom.

l: Callidice, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians, asks Ulysses to remain and gives him the kingdom. She bears him a son, Polypoetes; after she dies, Ulysses gives the kingdom to their son and returns to Ithaca.

s: Ulysses returns to Ithaca after being sent home by the Phaeacians and finds his household consumed by the suitors. He disguises himself as a beggar, reunites with Telemachus, kills the suitors, and is recognized by Penelope and Laertes. He later returns again after leaving the Thesprotians.

l: slaughter of the suitors, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Ulysses carries out the slaughter of the suitors with Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Telemachus after winning the contest of the bow. He also kills Melanthius and the handmaids who had slept with the suitors.

l: Penelope’s weaving ruse, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Penelope promises to marry after finishing Laertes’s shroud. She weaves it by day and undoes it by night for three years, deceiving the suitors until they discover what she is doing.

l: Poseidon, The Library, TOY Σειρήνων. αἱ δὲ Σειρῆνες ἦσαν Αχελῴου
s: Poseidon is angered by Ulysses and by the Phaeacians’ aid to him. He breaks apart Ulysses’s raft and turns the Phaeacians’ ship to stone, while enveloping their city with a mountain. Ulysses later propitiates Poseidon among the Thesprotians according to Tiresias’s directions.
